nameStory: German chamomile gets its name from the Greek words 'chamos' meaning ground and 'melos' meaning apple, referring to its sweet, apple-like fragrance when you crush the flowers or leaves. Despite being called 'German,' this cheerful little daisy actually originated in southern and eastern Europe, but it became so beloved in Germany for tea-making that it earned this geographical nickname.
description: German chamomile is a delicate annual herb that looks like a tiny white daisy with a bright yellow center. The plants grow 8-24 inches tall with feathery, finely-divided leaves that give them a soft, lacy appearance. These cheerful flowers bloom from late spring through fall, creating small clouds of sweet-scented white petals that are perfect for making the famous chamomile tea.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white daisy-like flowers with bright yellow centers that smell sweetly of apples when crushed - the fragrance is unmistakable and delightful

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Feathery, finely-divided leaves that feel soft and delicate to touch, resembling green lace with thread-like segments

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Branching annual herb growing 8-24 inches tall with multiple stems spreading from the base, creating bushy clusters

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Flower centers are hollow and cone-shaped when cut open, unlike solid centers of similar daisies

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny brown seeds without fluffy attachments, scattered when the spent flower heads are shaken

habitat: German chamomile thrives in disturbed soils like roadsides, gardens, fields, and waste areas throughout New England. It prefers sunny locations with well-drained, sandy or loamy soil and often appears as a garden escape or in areas where soil has been recently turned.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their characteristic feathery foliage, and early flowers may begin blooming in late spring in warmer locations.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with abundant white daisy flowers producing that distinctive apple-sweet fragrance - perfect time for tea harvesting.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering until first frost, with later flowers producing seeds for next year's plants.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: When you step on German chamomile, it releases such a strong apple-honey fragrance that in medieval times, people planted it in walkways as natural 'carpet deodorizer' - the more you walked on it, the better your garden smelled!
confusionNotes: Often confused with English daisy or other small white flowers, but German chamomile's sweet apple scent when crushed is unique - if it doesn't smell like apples, it's not chamomile! The hollow, cone-shaped flower centers also distinguish it from most look-alikes.
contextualKnowledge: While widely promoted as a calming tea, German chamomile can cause allergic reactions in people sensitive to plants in the daisy family (ragweed, chrysanthemums, marigolds). Always exercise caution when trying wild plants, and never consume anything you haven't identified with 100% certainty.
compareHints: German chamomile differs from its close relative pineapple-weed by having white petals around yellow centers, while pineapple-weed has only yellow-green dome-shaped flowers with no petals. Both share the sweet fragrance when crushed, but German chamomile's classic daisy appearance makes it much more recognizable to most people.

relatedSpecies.distinction: German chamomile, its closest relative in the same genus, has classic white daisy petals surrounding yellow centers and smells more like apples than pineapple.
